claims.claim: people understand your intent, not just your words.
No voice or face: readers fill gaps with their mood.

Short messages read as cold; jokes read as
serious; "Can we talk?" causes panic.
"Quick question about the invoice: is the date right?" beats "Is this right?"
"Could you…", "When you have a moment…", "Thanks!" costs nothing.

"Per my last email", "As I already said", "Just to be clear" sound passive-
  aggressive.
a full stop on a one-word chat reply ("Fine.") can read as annoyed;

exclamation marks
  in moderation sound warm;
ALL CAPS is shouting; "???" is impatient.
**Specific praise and thanks** in public, criticism in private and by voice.
**Re-read before sending** as the recipient: would it worry, hurt or confuse?
reply in threads, @mention only those who need to act, don't argue in the group.

Disagreement after two exchanges, bad news, emotional topics, complex decisions: call or meet, then
confirm the outcome in writing.
Directness varies; be clear and polite, avoid idioms and sarcasm with international colleagues.
Your last tricky message would read fine if forwarded to someone else or read aloud.

coverage: I extracted every concrete claim in the skill - the goal statement, the why-text-goes-wrong sentence, all seven practical-rules bullets (the context-first example, the softening phrases, the three passive-aggressive phrases with the restatement advice, the three punctuation effects, praise-and-criticism channels, re-read-as-recipient, and the group-chat rules), the four switch-channel triggers with call-or-meet-then-confirm-in-writing, the cultural directness/idioms/sarcasm rule, and the verify checklist item - and checked each against the skill's three listed sources: the JRC DigComp 2.2 publication page and the ICDL programmes page were fetched and read in full, while https://www.digitalliteracyassessment.org/ returned 403 Forbidden to automated fetches on every attempt and could not be read.
suggested_edits: None of the 16 concrete claims is stated by the two fetchable sources: the JRC page is the DigComp 2.2 framework, which frames netiquette only generically ("to be aware of behavioural norms and know-how while using digital technologies and interacting in digital environments. to adapt communication strategies to the specific audience and to be aware of cultural and generational diversity in digital environments") and never mentions punctuation effects, ALL CAPS, passive-aggressive phrases, praise/criticism channels, thread and @mention etiquette, or channel switching; the ICDL programmes page is a programme listing with no tone content; the third listed source blocks automated fetches with 403. Fix by citing pages that actually state each claim - netiquette or email-etiquette guides and research on how message tone is perceived (full stops on one-word chat replies, capitalisation read as shouting, phrase-level politeness), a source for moving disagreements and bad news to a call, and a source for cross-cultural directness, idioms and sarcasm - and drop https://www.digitalliteracyassessment.org/ (unfetchable) unless a specific fetchable page there covers a claim; keep DigComp 2.2 only as the framing source for the general netiquette advice.
